tagline: A tavern, a farmhouse and the Potomac trace Booth’s flight south.
intro: Booth’s Escape links Washington, D.C., with Southern Maryland’s towns, Zekiah Swamp and the Potomac River. Part of Maryland’s scenic-byway system, it follows several roads rather than a single historic highway. Visit Maryland presents the drive as a journey through the hiding places and escape route of Lincoln’s assassin. The tourism office also connects the corridor with Southern Maryland’s Underground Railroad sites, including the Port Tobacco jail, where enslaved freedom seekers were imprisoned.

On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in Washington and fled into Maryland. With David Herold, he collected weapons at the Surratt tavern, then reached Dr. Samuel Mudd’s home for treatment of his broken leg. At Bel Alton, Samuel Cox fed and sheltered the fugitives before sending them to hide in a pine thicket. Their flight continued toward the Potomac; federal troops caught up with them at a Virginia farm on April 26.

From Washington, the byway reaches Clinton and the Surratt House, then continues toward Waldorf and the Mudd farmhouse. Southward come Bryantown, St. Mary’s Church and Zekiah Swamp, followed by Bel Alton. Popes Creek Road brings the drive to the Potomac before the route continues toward the Virginia border.

moments.title: Surratt House, Clinton
moments.text: Two Spencer carbines hidden at the Surratt tavern belonged to an earlier plan to kidnap Lincoln. After the assassination, Booth and Herold stopped here to collect rifles and binoculars. Mary Surratt was convicted as a co-conspirator and hanged in 1865. The house later became a museum, opening to the public in 1976 after restoration. Its furnishings distinguish period setting from family possessions: the collection’s furniture did not belong to the Surratts, apart from Mary’s writing desk. The south addition is a reconstruction from the 1980s; the earlier addition did not survive.

moments.title: Dr. Samuel A. Mudd House
moments.text: The porch across this farmhouse’s front dates to 1928, decades after Booth came here with a broken leg. Mudd treated him on April 15, 1865. Booth and Herold slept in the front bedroom upstairs during a stay lasting between twelve and fifteen hours. The doctor’s later imprisonment involved more than that treatment: a military commission convicted him of aiding and conspiring in a murder. President Andrew Johnson pardoned Mudd, who left prison in 1869, but the conviction was never overturned. The house, also called St. Catharine, now operates as a historic house museum.
moments.notice: The farmhouse’s front porch was added in 1928.

moments.title: Popes Creek
moments.text: At Popes Creek, the byway reaches the Potomac shore where Booth’s escape became a river journey. Booth and Herold first rowed into Nanjemoy Creek by mistake and spent the night before crossing the Potomac later. The community lies north of the Harry Nice Memorial Bridge, with the crossing in sight from the shore. U.S. 301 runs north from the bridge, leaving Popes Creek between the highway and the river.
